p1.key: You need both volumes (mass of solution), both starting temperatures, the maximum temperature (ΔT) and the moles of NaOH (its concentration and volume). The HCl is in excess, so its concentration is not needed.
Doubling both volumes doubles the amount reacting (heat released) but also doubles the mass of solution being heated. ΔT = q/(mc) therefore stays at 6 °C.
Breaking bonds always needs energy, so H<sub>2</sub>O(g) → 2H(g) + O(g) is endothermic. Condensing, freezing and combustion all release heat.
Heat = mcΔT = y × c × z J (mass of water y g). Dividing by the amount dissolved (x mol) gives J mol−1: cyz/x.
The solution cools, so heat is taken in from the surroundings (the water): dissolving is endothermic and ΔH is positive.
q = mcΔT = 20 × 4.18 × 10 J; divide by 1000 for kJ. ΔT in °C equals ΔT in K, so 283 is not used.

p1.key: The temperature drops, so heat is absorbed from the surroundings: the reaction is endothermic and ΔH is positive.
A (thermal decomposition), B (ionization) and C (sublimation) are endothermic; D forms a Cl–Cl bond, which releases energy, so it is the only exothermic one.
H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is diprotic: the same amount of acid supplies twice as many H<sup>+</sup> ions, so twice as much water forms and twice the heat is released: Y = 2X.

An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings (I), so ΔH is positive (II). Statement III only holds when every species is gaseous; average bond enthalpies cannot describe all endothermic changes (e.g. dissolving or melting), so it is not always correct.
p1.flag: ms doubtful: III is true for gas-phase reactions, so D is arguable; earlier explanation gave D

p1.key: ΔH = −1204 kJ is for the equation as written: 2 mol Mg + 1 mol O<sub>2</sub> → 2 mol MgO, so 1204 kJ is released per 2 mol MgO (602 kJ per mol Mg or MgO; 1204 kJ per mol O<sub>2</sub>).
ΔH = −196 kJ refers to the equation as written, i.e. 2 mol SO2. The negative sign means energy is released, so per mole of SO2: 196 ÷ 2 = 98 kJ released.
Gas → solid (deposition) forms intermolecular attractions, so energy is released (exothermic). A (removing an electron from F⁻), B (breaking F–F) and C (ionization) all require energy.
Exothermic: products are at lower enthalpy than reactants, so ΔH is negative (I and II). Rate depends on activation energy, not on ΔH, so III is not true for all exothermic reactions.

In an endothermic reaction more energy is absorbed breaking reactant bonds than released forming product bonds, so the reactant bonds are stronger. The products have higher enthalpy (C wrong), and D describes ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0.
q = mcΔT, so m = q ÷ (cΔT) = 40 J ÷ (2.0 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 8.0 K) = 2.5 g.
Adding an electron to a gaseous Br atom (first electron affinity) releases energy. Atomization (A), ionization (B) and bond breaking (D) all absorb energy.

ΔT depends on (moles reacting) ÷ (mass of solution), so concentration must stay the same. B doubles both moles and volume, so ΔT stays at 6 °C. A doubles concentration (12 °C); C and D lower it (3 °C and 1.5 °C).
Halving both volumes halves the moles reacting (heat released) and halves the mass of solution being heated. ΔT = q/(mc) therefore stays the same: 6.4 °C.

q = mcΔT with m in kg to match c in kJ kg−1 K−1: q = 0.050 × 4.2 × 20 kJ. ΔH = −q/n = −(0.050 × 4.2 × 20)/0.10 kJ mol−1 (negative because the temperature rose). D. C forgets to convert grams to kilograms.
Neutralization (H+ + OH− → H2O forms bonds) and combustion always release heat. Decompositions are usually endothermic (e.g. CaCO3 → CaO + CO2). B: I and III only.

Calorimetry in an open beaker always loses heat to the surroundings, so the measured ΔT (and |ΔH|) is always too small: a systematic error in one direction. The other procedures use precise volumetric equipment with only small random errors. C.
Melting needs energy to overcome intermolecular forces (endothermic). Neutralization and combustion release heat. C: II and III only.

Mg is limiting in both beakers (0.05 g ≈ 0.002 mol; each beaker has 0.10 mol HCl), so the same amount of heat is released. In A that heat goes into half the mass of solution (100 cm3 vs 200 cm3), so ΔT = q/(mc) is twice as large: A.

The temperature rises, so the reaction is exothermic. The products are therefore at lower enthalpy and more stable. III is false: exothermic means the bonds formed in the products are stronger than those broken in the reactants.
Specific heat capacity is energy per unit mass per kelvin, so its units are energy ÷ (mass × temperature): kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
In both experiments 0.050 mol NaOH is neutralized (NaOH is limiting in B), so the same heat is released. B has a larger total volume (150 cm³), so its temperature rise is smaller.
All three are exothermic: combustion of methane (I), neutralization of the acidic aspirin by NaOH (II), and combustion of hydrogen (III).

The standard state of a substance is its pure form at the standard pressure of 100 kPa. Temperature is not part of the definition, though 298 K is usually quoted. The 298 °C in B and C is wrong anyway.

A 50 cm<sup>3</sup> pipette measures volume more precisely than a 100 cm<sup>3</sup> measuring cylinder, which reduces random error. Repeating the experiment reduces random error (not systematic), insulation reduces the systematic error from heat loss, and a larger volume does not increase systematic error.
The products are at lower enthalpy than the reactants, so heat is released (exothermic, ΔH negative). Lower enthalpy also means the products are more stable.
Removing an electron from a gaseous atom (ionization) always needs energy, so it is endothermic. Combustion, neutralization and condensation are all exothermic.
q = mcΔT = 10.0 g × 0.900 J g−1 K−1 × 20.0 K = +180 J. It is positive because the aluminium gains heat.
Combustion (I) and acid–base neutralization (III) release heat, so they are exothermic. Breaking the Cl–Cl bond (II) needs energy, so it is endothermic.
The products sit higher in enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH is positive and the reaction is endothermic: heat is absorbed. The lower-enthalpy reactants are the more stable species.

From q = mcΔT, ΔT = q/(mc). With q and m equal for every substance, the one with the smallest specific heat capacity has the largest temperature rise, so copper (0.39 J g−1 K−1) gets hottest. Al and NaCl have equal c, so they rise by the same amount.

Simple calorimetry in an uninsulated glass beaker loses a lot of heat to the surroundings. This systematic error is far larger than thermometer or burette errors, and it makes the measured ΔT and |ΔH| too small.

All three are exothermic. Neutralization (I) and combustion, here incomplete combustion to CO (II), release heat. Condensation of a gas to a liquid (III) also releases heat as intermolecular forces form.

n(NH4Cl) = 5.35 ÷ 53.5 = 0.100 mol. q = 25.0 × 4.18 × 14 J (use the solution mass; a temperature change in K needs no +273). The temperature fell, so the process is endothermic: ΔH = +25.0 × 4.18 × 14 ÷ (0.1 × 1000) kJ mol−1.
Moles needed = 683.5 ÷ 1367 = 0.500 mol. Mass = moles × Mr, so mass = 683.5 × 46.0 ÷ 1367 = 23.0 g.
The products are lower in enthalpy than the reactants, so heat is released and the reaction is exothermic. The lower-enthalpy products are more stable, so the reactants are the less stable species.

The products lie a distance z above the reactants, so ΔH = +z (endothermic). The catalysed path is the lower hump; its Ea is measured from the reactants to that peak: z up to the product level plus x, so Ea = x + z. A catalyst does not change ΔH.

In an endothermic reaction the products are higher in energy, so the climb to the transition state from the reactants (forward E<sub>a</sub>) is bigger than from the products (reverse E<sub>a</sub>): E<sub>a</sub>(forward) − E<sub>a</sub>(reverse) = ΔH > 0.
The products sit above the reactants, so the products have greater enthalpy, ΔH is positive and the reaction is endothermic.

Total volume is 200 cm<sup>3</sup>, so m = 200 g and q = 200 × 4.18 × y J. 0.010 mol of water forms, so ΔH = 200 × 4.18 × y ÷ (1000 × 0.010) kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (negative sign because the reaction is exothermic). A change in temperature has the same size in °C and K, so +273 is not needed.
ΔH is positive, so the reaction is endothermic: it absorbs heat from the surroundings and the temperature decreases. The products have higher enthalpy, so they are less stable than the reactants.
Same mass and same energy, so q = mcΔT gives c ∝ 1/ΔT. X warms half as much as Y (5 vs 10 °C), so X has twice the specific heat capacity of Y.

q = mcΔT uses the mass of water (100.0 g) and ΔT = 10.0 K (no +273 for a temperature change). Divide by the moles of ethanol (0.230/46.08) and by 1000 to get kJ; the sign is negative because the reaction is exothermic.

Large heat losses to the surroundings (open beaker, spirit burner flame) mean the measured temperature rise is much smaller than it should be, so the temperature change is the least accurate quantity. The masses are measured precisely on a balance, and Mr is a fixed value.
In an exothermic reaction heat flows from the system to the surroundings, so the products have lower enthalpy than the reactants (reactants > products, ΔH negative).
The products are lower in energy than the reactants, so energy is released (exothermic) and the products are the more stable (lower energy) species.
Mg (0.05 g ≈ 0.002 mol) is limiting in both (each has 0.10 mol HCl), so the same heat is released. X has half the volume (mass) of solution, so by q = mcΔT its temperature rise is twice as large.
ΔHf refers to 1 mol NH3; the equation forms 2 mol, so ΔH = 2 × (−46) = −92 kJ, i.e. 92 kJ released.
Second mix: 0.10 mol of each reactant (same as the first) so the same heat is released, but only 100 cm3 of solution instead of 200 cm3. Half the mass → double ΔT: 10 °C.
